title: Satyress’s centaur robot Threehalves has detailed rescue design claims, but no validated disaster-zone performance
summary: Satyress, a California robotics startup, says its teleoperation-based “superhumanoid” robot can be modularly repaired and has fail-safety features, but the available record does not show it operating successfully in disaster zones.

sources.title: What's happening with the Colorado River? Here's the breakdown.

claims.text: Under the 1922 Colorado River Compact, 7.5 million acre-feet was allocated each to the Upper Basin (Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, New Mexico) and Lower Basin (Arizona, California, Nevada), plus 1.5 million acre-feet to Mexico; the 1968 authorization of the Central Arizona Project gave Arizona the lowest priority within the Lower Basin.

sources.title: US Plan To Allocate Water From The Colorado River Will Severely Impact California, Arizona, & Nevada

claims.text: Under existing 'law of the river' priority, California holds the highest priority among Lower Basin states, so mandatory cuts fall most heavily on Arizona, particularly Central Arizona Project users (336-mile canal serving Phoenix/Tucson), where tribes have highest priority within CAP, followed by cities, with non-tribal agriculture lowest priority.

sources.title: US Plan To Allocate Water From The Colorado River Will Severely Impact California, Arizona, & Nevada

claims.text: Federal planning in 2026 contemplated cuts of up to 3 million acre-feet per year to Lower Basin deliveries under a 10-year framework reassessed every two years; a Lower Basin states voluntary proposal offered 1.25 million acre-feet per year for two years (Arizona 760,000, California 440,000, Nevada 50,000).

sources.title: US Plan To Allocate Water From The Colorado River Will Severely Impact California, Arizona, & Nevada

claims.text: USBR's September 2026 'most probable' 24-Month Study projected that with 6.0 million acre-feet released from Powell in water year 2027, Lake Powell could rise to 3,558.44 feet by June 2028 while Lake Mead could fall to 998.40 feet in August 2028.

claims.text: Under the 1922 Colorado River Compact Article III(a), 7.5 million acre-feet per annum was apportioned in perpetuity to the Upper Basin and 7.5 million acre-feet per annum to the Lower Basin for exclusive beneficial consumptive use, which shall include all water necessary for the supply of any rights which may now exist.

claims.text: Article III(c) of the 1922 Compact provides that if the United States recognizes a right in Mexico to Colorado River waters, such waters shall be supplied first from surplus over the aggregate of 7.5+7.5+1.0 maf, and any deficiency shall be equally borne by Upper and Lower Basins with Upper Division delivering at Lee Ferry one-half the deficiency; the 1944 Water Treaty Article 10 guarantees Mexico 1.5 million acre-feet per year, reduced proportionally only in extraordinary drought or serious accident to the U.S. irrigation system.

claims.text: Upper Colorado River Commission Feb 14 2026 consensus: Upper Basin states (CO, UT, WY, NM) agreed on durable long-term post-2026 operations, stating Upper Basin users face >2.0 MAF reductions and >40% of proven water rights in 2026 due to natural hydrologic shortage, and that Lower Basin demands seek water that does not exist.
